title: Diffusion-Driven State Space Models

paper.title: Diffusion-Driven State Space Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract In many domains, practitioners seek models that produce accurate forecasts while faithfully
capturing latent system dynamics.
Existing approaches typically sacrifice one of these goals: deep state space models often assume
Gaussian latent transitions, limiting fit and forecasting, while diffusion models are highly
expressive but lack principled inference for the underlying dynamics.
To combine the strengths of both, we introduce the Diffusion-Driven State Space Model (DDSSM),
which replaces the conventional Gaussian transition distribution with a diffusion model.
Our DDSSM resolves the open problem of how to jointly train an autoencoder and a diffusion model on
sequential data, thereby extending the literature on latent diffusion models for time series.
Moreover, we find that the DDSSM empirically outperforms a state-of-the-art deep SSM at fitting and
forecasting a simulated time series with multimodal transitions.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ) have emerged as a powerful class of generative models for high-dimensional data. For time series data, emerging evidence demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on forecasting, imputation, and sample-generation tasks ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , where diffusion models are typically used as generative samplers to produce future trajectories conditioned on past observations ( Su et al., 2025 ) . Some approaches perform diffusion directly in observation space ( Tashiro et al., 2021 ; Rasul et al., 2021 ; Kollovieh et al., 2023 ; Price et al., 2025 ) , while others apply diffusion in the latent space of an autoencoder ( Feng et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Blattmann et al., 2023 ) , which can improve tractability for high-dimensional data. However, existing latent time-series diffusion methods typically rely on two-stage training: first learning the autoencoder, then training the diffusion model. This may produce an over-regularized latent space ( Liu et al., 2024 ) that discards information needed for downstream generative dynamics, consistent with research on latent diffusion for static data where two-stage training leads to poorer representations and generative performance ( Vahdat et al., 2021 ; Shmakov et al., 2023 ) . In contrast, State Space Models (SSMs) ( Kalman, 1960 ; Shumway and Stoffer, 1982 ; Durbin and Koopman, 2001 ) provide a classical framework for temporal data that naturally supports end-to-end training, captures timestep-by-timestep dynamics, and admits well-studied extensions to diverse settings. SSMs typically assume observed data are generated from latent states that evolve over time via a Markov process, with each observation depending on the current state. Classically, the linear Gaussian state-space model assumes first-order Markovian linear dynamics and linear Gaussian observation models ( Roweis and Ghahramani, 1999 ) . To absolve linearity, transition and emission densities may be parameterized with deep neural networks ( Krishnan et al., 2015 ; Krishnan et al., 2017 ) , where training is performed via stochastic backpropagation ( Rezende et al., 2014 ; Kingma and Welling, 2014 ) . These neural-network-parameterized SSMs may be referred to as Deep SSMs, or Dynamical Variational Autoencoders (DVAEs); see Girin et al. (2022) for a review. While neural-networks allow the mean of each latent state to be a nonlinear function of the previous latent state, the transition densities in these models assume some parametric form ( Karl et al., 2016 ) , most often Gaussian ( Krishnan et al., 2015 ; Johnson et al., 2016 ; Fraccaro et al., 2017 ; Krishnan et al., 2017 ; Ansari et al., 2021 ; Girin et al., 2022 ; Revach et al., 2022 ; Dowling et al., 2024 ; Hashempoorikderi and Choi, 2024 ; Chinellato and Marcuzzi, 2025 ) , thereby limiting their expressivity. Moreover, Gaussian transition densities induce a Gaussian prior on the latent trajectories. Within the VAE framework the Gaussian prior is known to over-regularize, yielding latent representations that poorly represent the structure of the data ( Tomczak and Welling, 2018 ; Klushyn et al., 2019 ; Chen et al., 2017 ) . Inspired by the framework of composing probabilistic graphical models with neural networks ( Johnson et al., 2016 ) , we propose to get the “best of both worlds” by composing SSMs with diffusion models. Our diffusion-driven SSMs (DDSSMs) naturally model the real-time dynamics of a system without imposing restrictive Gaussian assumptions about its latent dynamics. Further, we adapt SSM ideas to resolve the open problem of how to jointly train an autoencoder and a diffusion model on sequential data in a principled manner. In this way, we extend latent diffusion models for time series.

sections.heading: Parameterization and Training.
sections.text: The design of the neural networks parameterizing these densities is detailed in Appendix H . We follow standard practice ( Girin et al., 2022 ) in minimizing the negative ELBO with stochastic backpropagation. To ensure the flow of gradients through the diffusion model to the VAE are normalized across noise levels, we use preconditioning ( Karras et al., 2022 ) as implemented in Section D.2 to rewrite Eq. 5a . Our full training algorithm, along with an explanation of how to compute each of the terms in the ELBO, can be found in Appendix I .

sections.heading: 3 Related work
sections.text: Deep state space models. Similarly to other Deep State Space Models (DSSMs) ( Girin et al., 2022 ) such as the Deep Kalman Filter (DKF) ( Krishnan et al., 2015 ; Krishnan et al., 2017 ) , our Diffusion-Driven State Space Model (DDSSM) parametrizes the transitions and emissions densities of a state space model with a neural network. However, our model replaces the parametric (typically Gaussian) transition distribution of a DSSM with a diffusion model. This design enables complex, potentially multi-modal transition dynamics (validated in Section 4 ) and avoids the restrictive regularization of Gaussian transitions ( Karl et al., 2016 ) . Integration with advances such as the extended Kalman filter VAE ( Klushyn et al., 2021 ) is left for future work. Diffusion models for temporal data. Some works ( Rasul et al., 2021 ; Tashiro et al., 2021 ; Kollovieh et al., 2023 ) apply diffusion directly in observation space, but the high computational cost of diffusion – motivating latent diffusion for static data ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) – is exacerbated in time series due to the need to model both high-dimensional structure and temporal dynamics. This has led to latent diffusion approaches for time series ( Qian et al., 2024 ; Suh et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Feng et al., 2024 ) , which typically rely on two-stage training (autoencoder then diffusion), potentially yielding over-regularized latent spaces that discard information needed for generative dynamics ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Vahdat et al., 2021 ; Shmakov et al., 2023 ) . Our approach instead follows Vahdat et al. (2021) and Shmakov et al. (2023) by training diffusion end-to-end in latent space, extended here to the temporal setting. For further details on related works, see Appendix J .

sections.heading: 5 Discussion
sections.text: In this work we have demonstrated that we can formulate latent diffusion models for time series by casting the problem as a state space model with a diffusion transition distribution. This allows end-to-end training, allowing flexible reconstructions without penalizing the learning of the latent dynamics. We aim to continue our work by applying the DDSSM to large-scale datasets, and by incorporating ideas from deep SSM literature to fully utilize the power of the diffusion transition distribution.

sections.heading: A.1 Derivation of the Generative Model
sections.text: Our goal is to learn a model of the conditional distribution p ( 𝐱 1 : T | 𝐮 1 : T ) p(\mathbf{x}_{1:T}|\mathbf{u}_{1:T}) . Following the general framework of Girin et al. (2022) , we introduce a sequence of latent variables 𝐳 1 : T = ( 𝐳 1 , 𝐳 2 , … , 𝐳 T ) \mathbf{z}_{1:T}=(\mathbf{z}_{1},\mathbf{z}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{z}_{T}) , where each 𝐳 t ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{z}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is a d d -dimensional vector, and factorize the joint distribution p ( 𝐱 1 : T , 𝐳 1 : T | 𝐮 1 : T ) p(\mathbf{x}_{1:T},\mathbf{z}_{1:T}|\mathbf{u}_{1:T}) as p ( 𝐱 1 : T , 𝐳 1 : T | 𝐮 1 : T ) = ∏ t = 1 T p ( 𝐱 t | 𝐱 1 : t − 1 , 𝐳 1 : t , 𝐮 1 : t ) p ( 𝐳 t | 𝐱 1 : t − 1 , 𝐳 1 : t − 1 , 𝐮 1 : t ) . p(\mathbf{x}_{1:T},\mathbf{z}_{1:T}|\mathbf{u}_{1:T})=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\mathbf{x}_{1:t-1},\mathbf{z}_{1:t},\mathbf{u}_{1:t})p(\mathbf{z}_{t}|\mathbf{x}_{1:t-1},\mathbf{z}_{1:t-1},\mathbf{u}_{1:t}). (6) We make the Markovian assumption that the latent state at time t t only depends on a fixed-length history of j j previous latent states and covariates, rather than the entire history, i.e. p ( 𝐳 t | 𝐳 1 : t − 1 , 𝐮 1 : t ) = p ( 𝐳 t | 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 , 𝐮 t − j : t ) , p\left(\mathbf{z}_{t}|\mathbf{z}_{1:t-1},\mathbf{u}_{1:t}\right)=p\left(\mathbf{z}_{t}|\mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1},\mathbf{u}_{t-j:t}\right), (7) for t > j t>j where j j is a fixed Markov order. On the emissions model, we assume that the observation at time t t only depends on a fixed-length history of j j previous latent states and covariates, i.e. p ( 𝐱 t | 𝐱 1 : t − 1 , 𝐳 1 : t , 𝐮 1 : t ) = p ( 𝐱 t | 𝐳 t − j + 1 : t , 𝐮 t − j + 1 : t ) . p(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\mathbf{x}_{1:t-1},\mathbf{z}_{1:t},\mathbf{u}_{1:t})=p(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\mathbf{z}_{t-j+1:t},\mathbf{u}_{t-j+1:t}). (8) We explicitly choose the same conditioning set for the emissions model, arguing that the most recent j j states carry the full information about the system’s current state, and thus the most recent j j states and covariates should be sufficient for predicting the current observation. Alternatively we could choose a smaller order on the emissions as well; this is not a key aspect of our model and leave this choice to future work. Lastly, we assume that the initial j j latent states are generated from a separate initial state distribution, i.e. p ( 𝐳 1 : j , 𝐱 1 : j | 𝐮 1 : j ) = p η ( 𝐳 1 : j | 𝐮 1 : j ) p θ ( 𝐱 1 : j | 𝐳 1 : j , 𝐮 1 : j ) . p(\mathbf{z}_{1:j},\mathbf{x}_{1:j}|\mathbf{u}_{1:j})=p_{\eta}(\mathbf{z}_{1:j}|\mathbf{u}_{1:j})p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{1:j}|\mathbf{z}_{1:j},\mathbf{u}_{1:j}). (9) Rewriting Eq. 6 with the above assumptions, we have p ( 𝐱 1 : T , 𝐳 1 : T | 𝐮 1 : T ) = \displaystyle p(\mathbf{x}_{1:T},\mathbf{z}_{1:T}|\mathbf{u}_{1:T})= p η ( 𝐳 1 : j | 𝐮 1 : j ) p θ ( 𝐱 1 : j | 𝐳 1 : j , 𝐮 1 : j ) ⏟ State Initialization \displaystyle\underbrace{p_{\eta}(\mathbf{z}_{1:j}|\mathbf{u}_{1:j})p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{1:j}|\mathbf{z}_{1:j},\mathbf{u}_{1:j})}_{\mathclap{\text{State Initialization}}} (10) × ∏ t = j + 1 T p ( t ) ψ ( 𝐳 t | 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 , 𝐮 t − j : t ) ⏟ Transition Density × p ( t ) θ ( 𝐱 t | 𝐳 t − j + 1 : t , 𝐮 t − j + 1 : t ) ⏟ Emissions Model , \displaystyle\times\prod_{t=j+1}^{T}\underbrace{p^{(t)}_{\psi}(\mathbf{z}_{t}|\mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1},\mathbf{u}_{t-j:t})\;}_{\mathclap{\text{Transition Density}}}\;\times\;\underbrace{p^{(t)}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\mathbf{z}_{t-j+1:t},\mathbf{u}_{t-j+1:t})}_{\mathclap{\text{Emissions Model}}}, where we have indicated the parameters as explained in the main text. The inclusion of j j as a hyperparameter for our model is inspired by the GenCast model of Price et al. (2025) , which found that a second-order Markov assumption (in observation space) was more effective for forecasting in contrast to a first-order assumption. We note that another option for increasing the Markov order would be to use a higher-dimensional latent state, where the transition density is still first-order in the latent space, but the latent state at time t t includes the previous j j states. However, the representation here allows for independently controlling the Markov order and the dimension of the latent state. Another motivation for this representation is that it allows us to view our method as a direct generalization of autoregressive diffusion models. For example, the model proposed by Price et al. (2025) can be viewed as our model with j = 2 j=2 and identity emissions.

sections.heading: Appendix B Modeling the Transition Density with Diffusion Models

To simplify notation, we will denote the history of latent states and covariates as 𝐜 t := ( 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 , 𝐮 t − j : t ) \mathbf{c}_{t}:=(\mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1},\mathbf{u}_{t-j:t}) , as this conditioning set remains fixed across the diffusion steps for a given time t t . Eq. 27 shows that we may write the transition density as p ψ ( t ) ( 𝐳 t | 𝐜 t ) = ∫ p ψ ( t ) ( 𝐳 t 0 | 𝐳 t 1 , 𝐜 t ) ∏ k = 2 K p ψ ( t ) ( 𝐳 t k − 1 | 𝐳 t k , 𝐜 t ) p ( 𝐳 t K ) d 𝐳 t 1 : K , p^{(t)}_{\psi}(\mathbf{z}_{t}|\mathbf{c}_{t})=\int p^{(t)}_{\psi}(\mathbf{z}_{t}^{0}|\mathbf{z}_{t}^{1},\mathbf{c}_{t})\;\prod_{k=2}^{K}p^{(t)}_{\psi}(\mathbf{z}_{t}^{k-1}|\mathbf{z}_{t}^{k},\mathbf{c}_{t})\;p(\mathbf{z}_{t}^{K})\;d\mathbf{z}_{t}^{1:K}, (11) where 𝐳 t 0 := 𝐳 t \mathbf{z}_{t}^{0}:=\mathbf{z}_{t} is the clean latent state, p ⁡ ( 𝐳 t K ) p(\mathbf{z}_{t}^{K}) has standard normal density, and p ψ ( t ) ( 𝐳 t k − 1 | 𝐳 t k , 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 ) p^{(t)}_{\psi}(\mathbf{z}_{t}^{k-1}|\mathbf{z}_{t}^{k},\mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1}) is the learned reverse process of the diffusion model. sections.heading: C.1 Posterior Factorization
sections.text: Learning our generative model in Eq. 12 requires performing inference over the latent variables 𝐳 1 : T \mathbf{z}_{1:T} and { 𝐳 t 1 : K } t = j + 1 T \{\mathbf{z}_{t}^{1:K}\}_{t=j+1}^{T} . To do so, we follow works from the deep state-space modeling literature ( Krishnan et al., 2015 ; Krishnan et al., 2017 ; Girin et al., 2022 ) and train under the VAE framework which allows jointly learning the generative model and the inference model. The primary objective is to maximize the marginal log-likelihood log p ( 𝐱 1 : T | 𝐮 1 : T ) \log p(\mathbf{x}_{1:T}|\mathbf{u}_{1:T}) with respect to the parameters of the generative model. As is typical with latent-variable models, exact inference depends on the smoothing posterior distribution p ( 𝐳 1 : T , { 𝐳 t 1 : K } t = j + 1 T ∣ 𝐱 1 : T , 𝐮 1 : T ) , p(\mathbf{z}_{1:T},\{\mathbf{z}_{t}^{1:K}\}_{t=j+1}^{T}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1:T},\mathbf{u}_{1:T}), (13) whose normalization involves integrating over a high-dimensional latent space and is generally intractable. To obtain a tractable objective, we introduce a variational distribution q ϕ ( 𝐳 1 : T , { 𝐳 t 1 : K } t = j + 1 T | 𝐱 1 : T , 𝐮 1 : T ) q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}_{1:T},\left\{\mathbf{z}_{t}^{1:K}\right\}_{t=j+1}^{T}|\mathbf{x}_{1:T},\mathbf{u}_{1:T}) (14) to approximate the true posterior distribution. It is important to choose a family of variational distributions which matches the conditional independence structure of the true posterior distribution ( Girin et al., 2022 ) . If the variational distribution misses important dependencies required to capture the true posterior, then the variational distribution will not be able to approximate the true posterior well, resulting in a looser bound on the marginal log-likelihood. Therefore, we examine the form of the true posterior distribution p ( 𝐳 1 : T , { 𝐳 t 1 : K } t = j + 1 T | 𝐱 1 : T , 𝐮 1 : T ) p(\mathbf{z}_{1:T},\{\mathbf{z}_{t}^{1:K}\}_{t=j+1}^{T}|\mathbf{x}_{1:T},\mathbf{u}_{1:T}) to determine the appropriate factorization for the variational distribution. The conditional independence structure of the true posterior distribution can be determined by applying d-separation to the directed graphical model corresponding to the generative model in Eq. 12 , resulting in the following lemma. Lemma 1 . For the generative model in Eq. 12 , the exact smoothing posterior factorizes as p ( 𝐳 1 : T , { 𝐳 t 1 : K } t = j + 1 T | 𝐱 1 : T , 𝐮 1 : T ) \displaystyle p(\mathbf{z}_{1:T},\{\mathbf{z}_{t}^{1:K}\}_{t=j+1}^{T}|\mathbf{x}_{1:T},\mathbf{u}_{1:T}) (15) = [ ∏ t = 1 j p ( 𝐳 t | 𝐱 t : T , 𝐳 1 : t − 1 , 𝐮 1 : t ) ] × [ ∏ t = j + 1 T p ( 𝐳 t | 𝐱 t : T , 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 , 𝐮 t − j : t ) ] \displaystyle\quad=\left[\prod_{t=1}^{j}p(\mathbf{z}_{t}|\mathbf{x}_{t:T},\mathbf{z}_{1:t-1},\mathbf{u}_{1:t})\right]\times\left[\prod_{t=j+1}^{T}p(\mathbf{z}_{t}|\mathbf{x}_{t:T},\mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1},\mathbf{u}_{t-j:t})\right] (16) × [ ∏ t = j + 1 T p ( 𝐳 t 1 : K | 𝐳 t , 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 , 𝐮 t − j : t ) ] , \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\times\left[\prod_{t=j+1}^{T}p(\mathbf{z}_{t}^{1:K}|\mathbf{z}_{t},\mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1},\mathbf{u}_{t-j:t})\right], (17) where p ( 𝐳 t 1 : K | 𝐳 t , 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 , 𝐮 t − j : t ) ∝ p ( 𝐳 t K ) ∏ k = 1 K p ψ ( t ) ( 𝐳 t k − 1 | 𝐳 t k , 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 , 𝐮 t − j : t ) , p(\mathbf{z}_{t}^{1:K}|\mathbf{z}_{t},\mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1},\mathbf{u}_{t-j:t})\propto p(\mathbf{z}_{t}^{K})\prod_{k=1}^{K}p^{(t)}_{\psi}(\mathbf{z}_{t}^{k-1}|\mathbf{z}_{t}^{k},\mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1},\mathbf{u}_{t-j:t}), (18) with 𝐳 t 0 := 𝐳 t \mathbf{z}_{t}^{0}:=\mathbf{z}_{t} . sections.heading: D.1 Background for Conditional Diffusion models
sections.text: Diffusion models are a class of generative models which learn to sample from some arbitrary data distribution by learning to reverse a gradual noising process. In the conditional setting, we wish to learn a model of the form p ⁡ ( 𝐱 | 𝐜 ) p(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{c}) , where 𝐜 \mathbf{c} is some conditioning information. To formulate the diffusion objective, we first must define a forward noising process. This process may be defined in either continuous or discrete time; we present the discrete-time case here. In discrete-time, the forward noising process is a Markov chain which gradually adds Gaussian noise to the data. As shown by Ho et al. (2020) , the forward noising process first takes an initial data point 𝐳 0 := 𝐳 \mathbf{z}^{0}:=\mathbf{z} sampled from the data, and then iteratively adds noise to produce a sequence of noisy latent states 𝐳 1 , 𝐳 2 , … , 𝐳 K \mathbf{z}^{1},\mathbf{z}^{2},\ldots,\mathbf{z}^{K} . The corruption process for each step k k is defined by a transition density q ⁡ ( 𝐳 k | 𝐳 k − 1 ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝐳 k , 1 − β k ​ 𝐳 k − 1 , β k ​ 𝐈 ) , q(\mathbf{z}^{k}|\mathbf{z}^{k-1})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{z}^{k};\sqrt{1-\beta_{k}}\mathbf{z}^{k-1},\beta_{k}\mathbf{I}), where 0 < β 1 , β 2 , … , β K < 1 0<\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\ldots,\beta_{K}<1 is a fixed noise schedule, The noise schedule is chosen such that the terminal latent state 𝐳 K \mathbf{z}^{K} is approximately distributed as 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 𝐈 ) \mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}) . This forward process allows direct sampling of a latent 𝐳 t k \mathbf{z}_{t}^{k} for some time step t t since q ⁡ ( 𝐳 t k | 𝐳 t 0 ) ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝐳 t k , α ¯ k ​ 𝐳 t 0 , ( 1 − α ¯ k ) ​ 𝐈 ) q(\mathbf{z}_{t}^{k}|\mathbf{z}_{t}^{0})\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{z}_{t}^{k};\sqrt{\overline{\alpha}_{k}}\mathbf{z}_{t}^{0},(1-\overline{\alpha}_{k})\mathbf{I}) , where α k = ( 1 − β k ) \alpha_{k}=(1-\beta_{k}) and α ¯ k = ∏ i = 1 k α i \overline{\alpha}_{k}=\prod_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_{i} . For data 𝐳 \mathbf{z} , a reversal process may be defined as p ψ ( t ) ​ ( 𝐳 k − 1 | 𝐳 k , 𝐜 ) , p^{(t)}_{\psi}\left(\mathbf{z}^{k-1}|\mathbf{z}^{k},\mathbf{c}\right), such that p ψ ( t ) ​ ( 𝐳 0 | 𝐜 ) \displaystyle p^{(t)}_{\psi}(\mathbf{z}^{0}|\mathbf{c}) = ∫ p ψ ( t ) ( 𝐳 0 : K − 1 | 𝐳 K , 𝐜 ) p ( 𝐳 K ) d 𝐳 1 : K \displaystyle=\int p^{(t)}_{\psi}\left(\mathbf{z}^{0:K-1}|\mathbf{z}^{K},\mathbf{c}\right)p(\mathbf{z}^{K})d\mathbf{z}^{1:K} = ∫ ∏ k = K 1 p ψ ( t ) ( 𝐳 k − 1 | 𝐳 k , 𝐜 ) p ( 𝐳 K ) d 𝐳 1 : K \displaystyle=\int\prod_{k=K}^{1}p^{(t)}_{\psi}\left(\mathbf{z}^{k-1}|\mathbf{z}^{k},\mathbf{c}\right)p(\mathbf{z}^{K})d\mathbf{z}^{1:K} (27) where p ψ ( t ) ​ ( 𝐳 k − 1 | 𝐳 k , 𝐜 ) p^{(t)}_{\psi}(\mathbf{z}^{k-1}|\mathbf{z}^{k},\mathbf{c}) is learned by a neural network with parameters ψ \psi . Typically, a single neural network with shared parameters ψ \psi is used to learn the reverse process across all noise levels, with the noise level k k fed in as an additional input to the network. Training this model can be accomplished by minimizing the variational bound on the negative log-likelihood of the data, we provide details in Section C.2 as this is key to our methodology. Sampling from the diffusion model is accomplished by first sampling 𝐳 K ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 𝐈 ) \mathbf{z}^{K}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}) , and then sampling 𝐳 K − 1 , 𝐳 K − 2 , … , 𝐳 0 \mathbf{z}^{K-1},\mathbf{z}^{K-2},\ldots,\mathbf{z}^{0} using the learned reverse process, however more efficient samplers are used in practice. We refer the reader to Ho et al. (2020) ; Song et al. (2020) ; Karras et al. (2022) for more details on diffusion models.

sections.heading: E.2 Preconditioning as a Variational Bound
sections.text: While training standard diffusion models, the signal-to-noise ratio of the noisy inputs to the diffusion model changes drastically across different noise levels. This results in the magnitude of the regression targets for the noise prediction model to fluctuate, and thus the magnitude of the gradients of the diffusion model to fluctuate drastically as well. As the diffusion model is being trained alongside the encoder and decoder, this results in high variance gradients for the encoder and decoder, which may lead to instability in training. To sidestep this issue and ensure stability of the gradients, we employ the preconditioning introduced by Karras et al. (2022) , where the proposed preconditioning re-scales the inputs and outputs of the neural network targets. This rescaling enforces that magnitudes are roughly unit variance across all noise levels, and thus the gradients of the diffusion model are more stable across noise levels. (2022) is a proper bound on the original log-likelihood log ⁡ p ψ ( t ) ​ ( 𝐳 t 0 | 𝐜 t ) \log p^{(t)}_{\psi}(\mathbf{z}_{t}^{0}|\mathbf{c}_{t}) , given proper weighting of the objective. (2021) also trains a diffusion model end-to-end in a VAE framework, and highlight this issue as well; during training of the encoder, Vahdat et al. (2021) choose to retain the weights so that the encoder is encouraged to match the true posterior of the diffusion model. Intuitively, this means that maximizing the ELBO penalizes errors in the noise prediction at small noise levels, where the signal-to-noise ratio is high. On the other hand, errors in noise prediction at large noise levels are not penalized as much, where the diffusion model is focused on denoising the lower-frequency structure of the sample. In the context of our full model, this property implies that the strongest regularization of the encoder comes from the small noise levels, penalizing the encoder for producing latent samples that cannot reveal the fine-grained structure of the data. sections.heading: Appendix F Experiment Details
sections.text: To ensure a fair comparison for our synthetic experiments, we fix architectural hyperparameters across the DKF and DDSSM models, and tune hyperparameters for both models using Optuna ( Akiba et al., 2019 ) . The only difference in architecture is the implementation for the transition model, where the DKF uses a Gaussian transition module and the DDSSM uses a conditional U-Net parameterized diffusion model. We provide identical search spaces to the tuning algorithm, using the one-step JSD as the evaluation metric on a validation set of examples.

sections.heading: Appendix G Variational Hierarchical Prior
sections.text: Klushyn et al. (2021) ; Klushyn et al. (2019) , consider the problem of defining the prior distribution over the initial latent state p ⁡ ( 𝐳 1 ) p(\mathbf{z}_{1}) in the j = 1 j=1 case. Typically, the prior is chosen by DSSMs to be a standard Gaussian Krishnan et al. (2015) ; Krishnan et al. (2017) ; Karl et al. (2016) . The prior over 𝐳 1 \mathbf{z}_{1} however regularizes the rest of the latent trajectory, as both the transition model and the encoder posterior are conditioned on 𝐳 1 \mathbf{z}_{1} . This is experimentally validated by Klushyn et al. (2019) ; Klushyn et al. (2021) , where it is demonstrated that a more flexible prior over the initial latent state can lead to better inference about the latent trajectory. As our diffusion transition model can be highly expressive, we wish to avoid inhibiting the expressiveness of the transition model by imposing a simple prior over the initial latent states. We therefore follow Klushyn et al. (2021) and use an expressive initial distribution via a variational hierarchical prior (VHP). In our case, we wish to handle higher Markov orders, so our initial state distribution is over the first j j latents, p ( 𝐳 1 : j ) p(\mathbf{z}_{1:j}) . For the j = 1 j=1 case, Klushyn et al. (2021) uses a two-level hierarchical prior, where the initial latent state 𝐳 1 \mathbf{z}_{1} is modeled as p ⁡ ( 𝐳 1 ) = ∫ p η ​ ( 𝐳 1 | 𝐳 0 ) ​ p ​ ( 𝐳 0 ) ​ d ​ 𝐳 0 , p(\mathbf{z}_{1})=\int p_{\eta}(\mathbf{z}_{1}|\mathbf{z}_{0})p(\mathbf{z}_{0})d\mathbf{z}_{0}, where p ⁡ ( 𝐳 0 ) p(\mathbf{z}_{0}) is a standard Gaussian. sections.heading: Appendix H Model Architecture Details
sections.text: The method of Tashiro et al. (2021) , titled “CSDI: Conditional Score-based Diffusion Models for Probabilistic Time Series Imputation”, uses a well-established architecture for modeling time-series data with diffusion models Tashiro et al. (2021) , and we adapt it to our setting of autoregressive generation in the latent space. We choose to extend the architecture of Tashiro, Song, Song and Ermon (2021) , for several reasons. First, it is a well-established architecture for modeling time-series data with diffusion models, Second, its success in modeling directly in observation space suggests that it is sufficiently powerful to model the transition distribution in latent space, and it is simple enough to allow us to modularize the architecture depending on the specific needs of the encoder, decoder, and transition modules. Specifically, we extend the U-net architecture from CSDI to not only our diffusion model, but also to the encoder, decoder, and initialization modules, which all operate on latent histories.

sections.heading: H.1 U-net Architecture
sections.text: Because we operate in the latent space and generate autoregressively, we utilize a static mask indicating which time steps functionally serve as the conditioning history versus the generated output, rather than a dynamic missing-data mask. Our mask is thus a binary mask 𝐦 hist \mathbf{m}_{\mathrm{hist}} of shape ( j + 1 ) (j+1) , which equals one for history steps and zero for the target step, since we are always generating a single step and conditioning on j j history steps. The input to the denoiser is a tensor 𝐙 ∈ ℝ M × ( j + 1 ) \mathbf{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times(j+1)} , where M M is the latent dimension. The target noise is always located at the last time step, while the clean history is located in the preceding j j time steps.

sections.heading: Input Projection
sections.text: Following Tashiro et al. (2021) , we separate the input into two components via the mask: a clean history 𝐙 hist = 𝐙 ⊙ 𝐦 hist \mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{hist}}=\mathbf{Z}\odot\mathbf{m}_{\mathrm{hist}} and a noisy target 𝐙 noisy = 𝐙 ⊙ ( 1 − 𝐦 hist ) \mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{noisy}}=\mathbf{Z}\odot(1-\mathbf{m}_{\mathrm{hist}}) . These are concatenated along a new channel dimension to form a tensor in ℝ 2 × M × ( j + 1 ) \mathbb{R}^{2\times M\times(j+1)} . A 1 × 1 1\times 1 convolution and a ReLU activation project this input to a hidden channel dimension C C , yielding an initial representation 𝐇 0 ∈ ℝ C × M × ( j + 1 ) \mathbf{H}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times M\times(j+1)} .

sections.heading: Extra Conditioning Information
sections.text: Conditioning is injected via a continuous diffusion timestep embedding and a side information tensor. The scalar diffusion noise level is embedded via sinusoidal positional encodings and a two-layer multi-layer perceptron into 𝐞 diff ∈ ℝ E diff \mathbf{e}_{\mathrm{diff}}\in\mathbb{R}^{E_{\mathrm{diff}}} . The side information tensor 𝐒 ∈ ℝ E side × M × ( j + 1 ) \mathbf{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{E_{\mathrm{side}}\times M\times(j+1)} concatenates dynamic covariates 𝐮 t − j : t \mathbf{u}_{t-j:t} , absolute time embeddings, and the mask 𝐦 hist \mathbf{m}_{\mathrm{hist}} . Since this diffusion operates on compressed latents rather than the original explicitly meaningful observation coordinates, in contrast to Tashiro et al. (2021) , we do not utilize static feature embeddings here.

sections.heading: Residual Blocks
sections.text: The core of our network consists of L L stacked residual blocks, each of which takes in a representation of shape ( C , M , j + 1 ) (C,M,j+1) and produces an output of the same shape as well as a skip connection. The residual block itself is mostly unchanged from CSDI, except we abstract the time-mixing and feature-mixing operations. This allows us to replace computationally heavy attention operations with architectures like a 1D convolution stack or a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) when the sequence length j j is small. We refer the reader to Tashiro et al. (2021) for more details on the architecture of the residual block.

sections.heading: Output Projection
sections.text: We continue to follow CSDI for handling the residual block inputs and outputs, as well as the skip connections. However, we deviate from CSDI in the output projection step. Because we generate autoregressively, we only need to produce an output for the target time step, rather than a full sequence of length j + 1 j+1 . So, we slice the final output of the residual block stack to only keep the target time step, yielding a tensor of shape ( M ) (M) , containing the predicted noise for the target time step.

sections.heading: H.2 Context Producer
sections.text: The encoder, decoder and initialization module, similar to the denoiser, operate on latent histories. Therefore for the encoder, decoder, and initialization module, we adapt the U-net architecture above as a general input-output architecture, where the inputs and outputs are tensors of shape ( h , L ) (h,L) for some hidden dimension h h and sequence length L L . The encoder, decoder, and initialization modules process sequential latent and observable data histories. To support this repetition, we abstract the U-net framework into a generalized feature-extraction module, which we call the Context Producer . The Context Producer accepts inputs of shape ( H seq , L ) (H_{\mathrm{seq}},L) , where H seq H_{\mathrm{seq}} is the spatial or feature dimension and L L is the temporal sequence length. The output is a vector representing the entire trajectory.

sections.heading: Input Projection
sections.text: Unlike the denoiser which separates clean and noisy data, the Context Producer takes a single sequence tensor 𝐇 in ∈ ℝ H seq × L \mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{in}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H_{\mathrm{seq}}\times L} . We treat this input sequence as having a single channel, flattening it temporarily to shape ( 1 , H seq × L ) (1,H_{\mathrm{seq}}\times L) , and apply a 1 × 1 1\times 1 convolution followed by a ReLU activation. This projects the input to a hidden channel dimension C C , yielding an initial representation 𝐇 0 ∈ ℝ C × H seq × L \mathbf{H}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times H_{\mathrm{seq}}\times L} .

sections.heading: Extra Conditioning Information
sections.text: Because the Context Producer does not reverse a diffusion process, we completely omit the diffusion step embedding. As with the denoiser, we inject conditioning information via a side information tensor, but we adapt the construction of this tensor to a side-information tensor 𝐒 ∈ ℝ E side × H seq × L \mathbf{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{E_{\mathrm{side}}\times H_{\mathrm{seq}}\times L} , where E side E_{\mathrm{side}} is the side information embedding dimension. We carefully construct this tensor to support both temporal and static covariates, as well as absolute time embeddings and the history/target mask. To construct the tensor we handle temporal and static information separately, and then concatenate them along the feature dimension. For each type of information we have: • Temporal Information. Dynamic covariates, time embeddings, and valid/padding masks vary over time L L but are uniform across the feature dimension H seq H_{\mathrm{seq}} . These are computed as a tensor of shape ( E time + E mask , L ) (E_{\mathrm{time}}+E_{\mathrm{mask}},L) and expanded along the feature dimension to ( E time + E mask , H seq , L ) (E_{\mathrm{time}}+E_{\mathrm{mask}},H_{\mathrm{seq}},L) . • Static Information. Static categorical or contextual embeddings vary across the features but are constant across time. These are mapped to a tensor ( E static , H seq ) (E_{\mathrm{static}},H_{\mathrm{seq}}) and expanded along the time dimension to ( E static , H seq , L ) (E_{\mathrm{static}},H_{\mathrm{seq}},L) . We concatenate the temporal and static information along the feature dimension to yield the final side information tensor 𝐒 ∈ ℝ E side × H seq × L \mathbf{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{E_{\mathrm{side}}\times H_{\mathrm{seq}}\times L} where E side = E time + E mask + E static E_{\mathrm{side}}=E_{\mathrm{time}}+E_{\mathrm{mask}}+E_{\mathrm{static}} .

sections.heading: Residual Blocks
sections.text: The residual blocks of the context producer are unchanged from Section H.1 , except the diffusion embedding is omitted. The utilization of the side information tensor is unchanged.

sections.heading: Output Projection
sections.text: The rest of the architecture is unchanged from our denoiser adaptation, except we do not project the ( C , h , L ) (C,h,L) output back to ( 1 , h , L ) (1,h,L) before slicing as we wish to produce a dense summary of the input rather than a noise prediction for a single time step. To concisely collapse the temporal dimension, we reshape the tensor equivalently to ( C × H seq , L ) (C\times H_{\mathrm{seq}},L) and apply a 1D convolution over the time dimension. Standard 1D convolutions would mix representations across the feature dimension, so we strictly use a grouped 1D convolution with groups equal to C × H seq C\times H_{\mathrm{seq}} and a kernel size equal to the sequence length L L . This operation pools the sequence, outputting a flattened context vector in ℝ C × H seq \mathbb{R}^{C\times H_{\mathrm{seq}}} .

sections.heading: H.3 Decoder Architecture
sections.text: The decoder architecture parameterizes the emissions density p θ ( t ) ( 𝐱 t | 𝐳 t − j + 1 : t , 𝐮 t − j + 1 : t ) p^{(t)}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\mathbf{z}_{t-j+1:t},\mathbf{u}_{t-j+1:t}) as a diagonal Gaussian distribution over the observation 𝐱 t ∈ ℝ D \mathbf{x}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} . It takes the sequential latent history and extracts a summary using a Context Producer to predict the observation parameters.

sections.heading: Input Preparation
sections.text: The inputs include the length- j j latent history 𝐳 t : t − j + 1 \mathbf{z}_{t:t-j+1} and covariates 𝐮 t − j + 1 : t \mathbf{u}_{t-j+1:t} . For early time steps where t < j t<j , the available history is left-padded with zero vectors to strongly enforce a fixed sequence length j j . We include a binary mask to indicate which time steps are padded versus valid, and add this to the set of conditioning information. The resulting sequence of shape ( M , j ) (M,j) is processed step-wise by a linear layer mapping the latent dimension M M to the Context Producer’s spatial dimension H seq H_{\mathrm{seq}} . This outputs the primary input sequence 𝐇 in ∈ ℝ H seq × j \mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{in}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H_{\mathrm{seq}}\times j} for the Context Producer.

sections.heading: Conditioning Construction
sections.text: The decoder’s Context Producer requires side information aligned to its j j -step temporal axis: • Temporal Information: We compute absolute time embeddings for the j j history steps. These are concatenated with the step-aligned dynamic covariates 𝐮 t − j + 1 : t \mathbf{u}_{t-j+1:t} . As previously mentioned, we embed a binary padding mask—which flags valid history vectors versus left-padded zero vectors—into a continuous embedding space. • Static Information: If static observation-level covariates are present, they are linearly projected from the data dimension D D to the spatial hidden dimension H seq H_{\mathrm{seq}} . The purpose of this projection is to ease the decoder’s task of matching its generated data to observed data, since the semantically meaningful static covariates are in the data space rather than the latent space. These elements are integrated as the side information tensor 𝐒 \mathbf{S} utilizing the mechanisms defined in Section H.2 .

sections.heading: Gaussian Output
sections.text: The Context Producer condenses the sequence into a final structured summary vector of shape ( C × H seq ) (C\times H_{\mathrm{seq}}) . Because the Context Producer utilizes several non-linear residual blocks, we preserve a residual path for available static covariates by mapping the flattened static covariates through an auxiliary linear layer and adding the result directly to the summary vector. This resulting context vector is passed into the Gaussian output head, which comprises two multi-layer perceptrons producing the distribution parameters: the mean μ θ ​ ( 𝐫 t ) ∈ ℝ D \mu_{\theta}(\mathbf{r}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{D} and the log-variance log ⁡ Σ θ ​ ( 𝐫 t ) ∈ ℝ D \log\Sigma_{\theta}(\mathbf{r}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{D} for the components of 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} .

sections.heading: H.4 Encoder Architecture
sections.text: The encoder approximates the smoothed variational density q ϕ ( t ) ( 𝐳 t | 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 , 𝐱 1 : T , 𝐮 t − j : t ) q^{(t)}_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}_{t}|\mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1},\mathbf{x}_{1:T},\mathbf{u}_{t-j:t}) . As mentioned in Section C.1 , we simplify the conditioning set by summarizing all future information into a sequence of continuous vectors 𝐡 1 : T \mathbf{h}_{1:T} , i.e. our variational family assumes q ϕ ( t ) ( 𝐳 t | 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 , 𝐮 t − j : t , 𝐱 t : T ) ≈ q ϕ ( t ) ( 𝐳 t | 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 , 𝐮 t − j : t , 𝐡 t ) q^{(t)}_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}_{t}|\mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1},\mathbf{u}_{t-j:t},\mathbf{x}_{t:T})\approx q^{(t)}_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}_{t}|\mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1},\mathbf{u}_{t-j:t},\mathbf{h}_{t}) . Therefore, there are two stages to our encoder’s operation: (i) a full-sequence Future Summary module that processes the entire future trajectory to produce a sequence of future summaries 𝐡 1 : T \mathbf{h}_{1:T} , and (ii) an autoregressive Context Producer that takes in the current latent history and the current future summary to produce the parameters of the variational distribution over z t z_{t} . We provide the algorithmic details of sampling a full trajectory from the encoder in Algorithm 2 .

sections.heading: Future Summary Module
sections.text: The Future Summary module computes 𝐡 1 : T = F ϕ ( 𝐱 1 : T , 𝐦 obs ) \mathbf{h}_{1:T}=F_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_{1:T},\mathbf{m}_{\mathrm{obs}}) . At each time step across the length- T T sequence, we concatenate the observations 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} , absolute time embeddings, observation missingness masks 𝐦 obs , t \mathbf{m}_{\mathrm{obs},t} , and the flattened static covariates. This feature vector is linearly projected to a hidden dimension C summary C_{\mathrm{summary}} . In line with Krishnan et al. (2017) , to ensure that 𝐡 t \mathbf{h}_{t} only absorbs information from the future and present (time t ​ … ​ T t\dots T ), the entire projected sequence is reversed along the time dimension and passed through a causal sequence model (such as a Gated Recurrent Unit or a causally-masked Transformer). The output sequence is reversed again, restoring the original chronological order while guaranteeing that 𝐡 t ∈ ℝ C summary \mathbf{h}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{C_{\mathrm{summary}}} depends only on sequence indices ≥ t \geq t .

sections.heading: Input Preparation
sections.text: Given the future summary 𝐡 t \mathbf{h}_{t} , the encoder autoregressively infers the parameters for 𝐳 t \mathbf{z}_{t} contingent on previously sampled states 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 \mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1} . For the first j j time steps, we left-pad the latent history with zero vectors and include a binary mask to indicate which time steps are padded versus valid, and add this to the set of conditioning information. This is the same strategy taken by the decoder (see Section H.3 ). We linearly project the future summary from C summary C_{\mathrm{summary}} to the Context Producer spatial dimension H seq H_{\mathrm{seq}} . Likewise, the j j history vectors are mapped from the latent dimension M M to H seq H_{\mathrm{seq}} . These are concatenated along the temporal axis to yield the primary input tensor 𝐇 in ∈ ℝ H seq × ( j + 1 ) \mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{in}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H_{\mathrm{seq}}\times(j+1)} for the Context Producer, where the future summary is located at index 0 0 and the history vectors are located at indices 1 ​ … ​ j 1\dots j . By placing the future summary at the beginning of the sequence, we allow the Context producer to attend to the future summary at each layer of its architecture. This choice is once again inspired by Krishnan et al. (2017) , who project the future summary to the initial hidden state of their RNN-based encoder, which allows the future summary to influence the entire inference process. In fact, this is the behavior of the Context Producer when we use an RNN for the time-mixing operation in the residual blocks.

sections.heading: Conditioning Construction
sections.text: The side information for the encoder’s Context Producer includes absolute time embeddings for the j j history steps, as well as a binary mask indicating which of the j j history steps are valid versus left-padded, and dynamical covariates for the j j history steps. We additionally include static covariates, and similar to the encoder we project these from the data space to the Context Producer’s spatial dimension to ease the task of matching the generated latent states to the observed data. To summarize these inputs, we have: • Temporal & Covariate Information: We gather absolute time embeddings and dynamic covariates aligned with the exact ( j + 1 ) (j+1) slots: time t t for the summary slot, and t − j ​ … ​ t − 1 t-j\dots t-1 for the history slots. • Role Mask: We employ a binary mask—set to 0 0 for the future summary slot and 1 1 for the history slots—which is projected through a learned linear layer. This explicitly instructs the residual blocks to treat the two modalities differently. • Padding Mask: We use an additional binary mask representing valid versus zero-padded history steps, which is also passed through a learned embedding layer. • Static Information: Similar to the decoder, static categorical or continuous covariates are mapped to the spatial attribute H seq H_{\mathrm{seq}} and expanded identically across the temporal axis.

sections.heading: Gaussian Output
sections.text: The sequence 𝐇 in \mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{in}} and side information 𝐒 \mathbf{S} are evaluated through the Context Producer described in Section H.2 , returning a flattened representation vector in ℝ C × H seq \mathbb{R}^{C\times H_{\mathrm{seq}}} . Finally, this vector is processed by a Gaussian MLP head to produce the mean μ t ∈ ℝ M \mu_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{M} and diagonal log-variance log ⁡ Σ t ∈ ℝ M \log\Sigma_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{M} defining the variational posterior for 𝐳 t \mathbf{z}_{t} .

sections.heading: H.5 Transition Architecture (Baselines)
sections.text: The Gaussian baseline transition model parameterizes p ψ ( t ) ( 𝐳 t | 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 , 𝐮 t − j : t ) p^{(t)}_{\psi}(\mathbf{z}_{t}|\mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1},\mathbf{u}_{t-j:t}) as a diagonal Gaussian, where the mean and log-variance are produced by a Context Producer followed by a Gaussian MLP head.

sections.heading: Input Preparation
sections.text: The transition model receives only the length- j j latent history 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 \mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1} as input (no future summary or observation information). Each latent vector 𝐳 t − i ∈ ℝ M \mathbf{z}_{t-i}\in\mathbb{R}^{M} is linearly projected to the Context Producer’s spatial dimension H seq H_{\mathrm{seq}} , yielding the primary input tensor 𝐇 in ∈ ℝ H seq × j \mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{in}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H_{\mathrm{seq}}\times j} . Unlike the encoder, no padding is required: the transition model is only invoked for t > j t>j , so a full history of length j j is always available.

sections.heading: Conditioning Construction
sections.text: Because the transition model has no future summary and no padded positions, its side information is considerably simpler than the encoder’s: • Temporal Information: Absolute time embeddings for the j j history steps t − j , … , t − 1 t-j,\ldots,t-1 are gathered and, if dynamic covariates 𝐮 t − j : t \mathbf{u}_{t-j:t} are present, concatenated along the feature dimension. • Mask Information: No mask embeddings are used. The Context Producer receives a zero-dimensional mask tensor (i.e. mask_tot_dim = 0 =0 ), so no role mask or padding mask is injected. • Static Information: No static covariates are provided, since the transition operates entirely in the latent space and does not need to align with observation-level features.

sections.heading: Gaussian Output
sections.text: The Context Producer condenses the history into a flattened context vector in ℝ C × H seq \mathbb{R}^{C\times H_{\mathrm{seq}}} , which is passed to a Gaussian MLP head producing the mean μ ψ ( 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 ) ∈ ℝ M \mu_{\psi}(\mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1})\in\mathbb{R}^{M} and diagonal log-variance log Σ ψ ( 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 ) ∈ ℝ M \log\Sigma_{\psi}(\mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1})\in\mathbb{R}^{M} . The transition density is then p ψ ( t ) ( 𝐳 t | 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 , 𝐮 t − j : t ) = 𝒩 ( 𝐳 t ; μ ψ ( 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 ) , diag ( exp log Σ ψ ( 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 ) ) ) . p^{(t)}_{\psi}(\mathbf{z}_{t}|\mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1},\mathbf{u}_{t-j:t})=\mathcal{N}\!\left(\mathbf{z}_{t};\;\mu_{\psi}(\mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1}),\;\operatorname{diag}\!\left(\exp\log\Sigma_{\psi}(\mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1})\right)\right).

sections.heading: H.6 VHP Architecture
sections.text: The variational hierarchical prior (VHP) for the initial latent states p η ( 𝐳 1 : j | 𝐳 − j + 1 : 0 ) p_{\eta}(\mathbf{z}_{1:j}|\mathbf{z}_{-j+1:0}) is implemented with two small Context Producers, one for the conditional prior p η p_{\eta} and one for the auxiliary variational posterior q Φ ( 𝐳 − j + 1 : 0 | 𝐳 1 : j ) q_{\Phi}(\mathbf{z}_{-j+1:0}|\mathbf{z}_{1:j}) . The architectures described below we implement with fewer layers and smaller hidden dimensions, given the simpler task of modeling only j j time steps rather than the full sequence of length T T . We refer to Appendix G for the mathematical derivation.

sections.heading: Conditional Prior p η ( 𝐳 t | 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 ) p_{\eta}(\mathbf{z}_{t}|\mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1})
sections.text: The conditional prior for t ≤ j t\leq j shares the same architecture as the Gaussian baseline transition described above: a Context Producer of temporal length j j followed by a Gaussian MLP head producing μ η , log ⁡ Σ η ∈ ℝ M \mu_{\eta},\log\Sigma_{\eta}\in\mathbb{R}^{M} . Its side information consists of absolute time embeddings, optional dynamic covariates, and an embedded padding mask, since during the autoregressive generation of 𝐳 1 , … , 𝐳 j \mathbf{z}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{z}_{j} , the conditioning history may include auxiliary latents 𝐳 − j + 1 : 0 \mathbf{z}_{-j+1:0} sampled from the VHP prior p ( 𝐳 − j + 1 : 0 ) = 𝒩 ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) p(\mathbf{z}_{-j+1:0})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) or from the auxiliary posterior q Φ q_{\Phi} . Concretely, at step t ∈ { 1 , … , j } t\in\{1,\ldots,j\} , the history 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 \mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1} is formed by concatenating the available auxiliary latents with any already-generated initial latents, left-padded with zeros when t < j t<j . A binary padding mask indicating which positions are real versus padded is embedded through a learned linear layer and injected as mask side information, exactly as in the encoder ( Section H.4 ).

sections.heading: Auxiliary Posterior q Φ ( 𝐳 − j + 1 : 0 | 𝐳 1 : j ) q_{\Phi}(\mathbf{z}_{-j+1:0}|\mathbf{z}_{1:j})
sections.text: The auxiliary posterior takes the encoder’s initial latent samples 𝐳 1 : j \mathbf{z}_{1:j} and produces a diagonal Gaussian over all j j auxiliary latents jointly. Each latent 𝐳 t \mathbf{z}_{t} for t ∈ { 1 , … , j } t\in\{1,\ldots,j\} is linearly projected from ℝ M \mathbb{R}^{M} to ℝ H seq \mathbb{R}^{H_{\mathrm{seq}}} , forming an input sequence of shape ( H seq , j ) (H_{\mathrm{seq}},j) for a second, smaller Context Producer. This Context Producer uses the same residual-block architecture described in Section H.2 , with temporal side information (absolute time embeddings and optional covariates for the first j j steps) but no mask embeddings ( mask_tot_dim = 0 =0 ), since the full sequence 𝐳 1 : j \mathbf{z}_{1:j} is always observed. The flattened output in ℝ C × H seq \mathbb{R}^{C\times H_{\mathrm{seq}}} is passed to a Gaussian MLP head that outputs the mean μ Φ ∈ ℝ M × j \mu_{\Phi}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times j} and diagonal log-variance log ⁡ Σ Φ ∈ ℝ M × j \log\Sigma_{\Phi}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times j} for the j j auxiliary latents. Sampling is performed via the reparameterization trick: 𝐳 − j + 1 : 0 = μ Φ ( 𝐳 1 : j ) + exp ( 1 2 log Σ Φ ( 𝐳 1 : j ) ) ⊙ ϵ , ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) . \mathbf{z}_{-j+1:0}=\mu_{\Phi}(\mathbf{z}_{1:j})+\exp\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\log\Sigma_{\Phi}(\mathbf{z}_{1:j})\right)\odot\bm{\epsilon},\qquad\bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}).

sections.heading: I.1 Parameters
sections.text: For clarity, we summarize the parameters being optimized in our model. The full parameter set consists of five groups: 1. Encoder parameters ϕ \phi : all parameters of the encoder Context Producer, Future Summary module, and Gaussian MLP head ( Section H.4 ). 2. Decoder parameters θ \theta : all parameters of the decoder network ( Section H.3 ). 3. Transition parameters ψ \psi : all parameters of the transition Context Producer and Gaussian MLP head ( Section H.5 ). 4. VHP conditional prior parameters η \eta : all parameters of the conditional prior Context Producer and Gaussian MLP head used to model p η ( 𝐳 t | 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 ) p_{\eta}(\mathbf{z}_{t}|\mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1}) for t ∈ { 1 , … , j } t\in\{1,\ldots,j\} ( Section H.6 ). 5. VHP auxiliary posterior parameters Φ \Phi : all parameters of the auxiliary posterior Context Producer and Gaussian MLP head used to model q Φ ( 𝐳 − j + 1 : 0 | 𝐳 1 : j ) q_{\Phi}(\mathbf{z}_{-j+1:0}|\mathbf{z}_{1:j}) ( Section H.6 ).

sections.heading: I.2 Optimization Techniques
sections.text: It is a well-known difficulty of VAEs that the optimization of the ELBO may be viewed as a multi-objective optimization problem, where the two competing objectives are the reconstruction of the data and the regularization of the latent space via the prior Higgins et al. (2017) ; Rezende and Viola (2018) . For example, in the most-general VAE setting, the ELBO may be written as ELBO ​ ( ϕ , θ ) = − 𝔼 q ϕ ​ ( 𝐳 | 𝐱 ) ​ [ log ⁡ p θ ( t ) ​ ( 𝐱 | 𝐳 ) ] + D KL ​ ( q ϕ ​ ( 𝐳 | 𝐱 ) ∥ p ⁡ ( 𝐳 ) ) , \text{ELBO}(\phi,\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})}[\log p^{(t)}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{z})]+D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})\,\middle\|\,p(\mathbf{z})\right), or in the distortion-rate form, ELBO ​ ( ϕ , θ ) = 𝒟 ⁡ ( ϕ , θ ) + ℛ ⁡ ( ϕ ) , \text{ELBO}(\phi,\theta)=\mathcal{D}(\phi,\theta)+\mathcal{R}(\phi), where the distortion term 𝒟 ⁡ ( ϕ , θ ) := − 𝔼 q ϕ ​ ( 𝐳 | 𝐱 ) ​ [ log ⁡ p θ ​ ( 𝐱 | 𝐳 ) ] \mathcal{D}(\phi,\theta):=-\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})}[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{z})] measures the reconstruction error, and the rate term ℛ ⁡ ( ϕ ) := D KL ​ ( q ϕ ​ ( 𝐳 | 𝐱 ) ∥ p ⁡ ( 𝐳 ) ) \mathcal{R}(\phi):=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})\,\middle\|\,p(\mathbf{z})\right) measures the complexity of the latent representation. It is commonplace in the VAE literature and the Deep SSM literature to employ a weighting term β \beta on the rate term to balance the tradeoff between reconstruction and regularization Higgins et al. (2017) ; Krishnan et al. (2017) , this is particularly important for DSSMs with learnable priors. To emphasize learning a good reconstruction before regularization, it is common to anneal β \beta from 0 0 to 1 1 during training. To avoid confusing notation with the diffusion schedule, we denote this regularization term as λ \lambda instead of β \beta . That is, we optimize the following objective: ℒ ELBO ( ϕ , η , θ , ψ , Φ ; 𝐱 1 : T , 𝐮 1 : T ) = 𝒟 ( ϕ , θ ) + λ ℛ ( ϕ , η , ψ , Φ ) , \mathcal{L}_{\text{ELBO}}(\phi,\eta,\theta,\psi,\Phi;\mathbf{x}_{1:T},\mathbf{u}_{1:T})=\mathcal{D}(\phi,\theta)+\lambda\mathcal{R}(\phi,\eta,\psi,\Phi), where the distortion term 𝒟 \mathcal{D} includes the reconstruction loss, and the rate term ℛ \mathcal{R} collects the posterior entropy, diffusion KL, any initialization likelihoods, and auxiliary posterior KL contributions. We utilize cosine annealing schedules for λ \lambda in our experiments. To find the optimal schedule, we use the hyperparameter λ end \lambda_{\text{end}} to specify the ending value of λ \lambda , and use the hyperparameter λ warmup \lambda_{\text{warmup}} to specify the number of training iterations until λ \lambda reaches λ end \lambda_{\text{end}} . Empirically, we find that choosing a good schedule is crucial for performance, hence we include these parameters in our hyperparameter sweep during training (see Section F.1.1 ).

sections.heading:
I.3 Computing MC
Estimates of ELBO Terms
sections.text: It still remains to detail the computation of the other ELBO terms, and to deal with the expectations in each term. When any of the distributions involved are Gaussian, computing the KL divergences becomes straightforward as the Gaussian distribution admits closed-form expressions for likelihoods and KL divergences. In the case of non-Gaussian distributions, we must use a Monte Carlo estimates to compute the various expectations. To allow us to reduce the error of the Monte Carlo estimates, we draw several latent trajectory samples from our encoder during training. Let the S S trajectories drawn from the encoder during training be denoted by 𝐳 1 : T ( s ) ∼ q ϕ ( 𝐳 1 : T ∣ 𝐱 1 : T , 𝐮 1 : T ) \mathbf{z}_{1:T}^{(s)}\sim q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}_{1:T}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1:T},\mathbf{u}_{1:T}) . We now detail the Monte-Carlo estimate for each term in the ELBO.

sections.heading: I.3.1 Initialization Loss
sections.text: Following the decomposition in Eq. 44 , we compute the initialization loss as the sum of the entropy term and the VHP loss. Using the sampled latent trajectories 𝐳 1 : T ( s ) \mathbf{z}_{1:T}^{(s)} , we first compute the entropy estimate: ℒ init entropy, MC ( ϕ ; 𝐱 1 : T , 𝐮 1 : T ) = 1 S ∑ s = 1 S log q ϕ ( 𝐳 1 : j ( s ) | 𝐱 1 : T , 𝐮 1 : T ) . \mathcal{L}_{\text{init}}^{\text{entropy, MC}}(\phi;\mathbf{x}_{1:T},\mathbf{u}_{1:T})=\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\log q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}_{1:j}^{(s)}|\mathbf{x}_{1:T},\mathbf{u}_{1:T}). (46) For the VHP loss, we sample auxiliary variables 𝐳 − j + 1 : 0 ( s ) ∼ q ϕ ( 𝐳 − j + 1 : 0 | 𝐳 1 : j ( s ) ) \mathbf{z}_{-j+1:0}^{(s)}\sim q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}_{-j+1:0}|\mathbf{z}_{1:j}^{(s)}) for each trajectory s s . The KL divergence term is computed analytically, assuming Gaussian distributions. ℒ VHP MC ( ϕ , η , Φ ; 𝐱 1 : T , 𝐮 1 : T ) \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{VHP}}^{\text{MC}}(\phi,\eta,\Phi;\mathbf{x}_{1:T},\mathbf{u}_{1:T}) = 1 S ∑ s = 1 S [ − ∑ t = 1 j log p η ( 𝐳 t ( s ) | 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 ( s ) ) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\Bigg[-\sum_{t=1}^{j}\log p_{\eta}(\mathbf{z}_{t}^{(s)}|\mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1}^{(s)}) + D KL ( q ϕ ( 𝐳 − j + 1 : 0 | 𝐳 1 : j ( s ) ) ∥ p ( 𝐳 − j + 1 : 0 ) ) ] , \displaystyle\qquad+D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}_{-j+1:0}|\mathbf{z}_{1:j}^{(s)})\,\middle\|\,p(\mathbf{z}_{-j+1:0})\right)\Bigg], (47) where the history 𝐳 t − j : t − 1 ( s ) \mathbf{z}_{t-j:t-1}^{(s)} in the reconstruction term draws from the auxiliary variables 𝐳 − j + 1 : 0 ( s ) \mathbf{z}_{-j+1:0}^{(s)} when indices are non-positive. The total initialization loss is ℒ init MC = ℒ init entropy, MC + ℒ VHP MC . \mathcal{L}_{\text{init}}^{\text{MC}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{init}}^{\text{entropy, MC}}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{VHP}}^{\text{MC}}. (48)

sections.heading: I.3.2 Sequence Reconstruction Loss
sections.text: For the reconstruction loss, we use the same sampled latent trajectories 𝐳 1 : T ( s ) ∼ q ϕ ( 𝐳 1 : T ∣ 𝐱 1 : T , 𝐮 1 : T ) \mathbf{z}_{1:T}^{(s)}\sim q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}_{1:T}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1:T},\mathbf{u}_{1:T}) as above. Our decoder is Gaussian, and given most generally by p θ ( t ) ( 𝐱 t ∣ 𝐳 max ⁡ ( 1 , t − j + 1 ) : t , \displaystyle p^{(t)}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{z}_{\max(1,t-j+1):t}, 𝐮 max ⁡ ( 1 , t − j + 1 ) : t ) = \displaystyle\mathbf{u}_{\max(1,t-j+1):t})= 𝒩 ( μ θ ( 𝐳 max ⁡ ( 1 , t − j + 1 ) : t , 𝐮 max ⁡ ( 1 , t − j + 1 ) : t ) , Σ θ ( 𝐳 max ⁡ ( 1 , t − j + 1 ) : t , 𝐮 max ⁡ ( 1 , t − j + 1 ) : t ) ) , \displaystyle\mathcal{N}(\mu_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{\max(1,t-j+1):t},\mathbf{u}_{\max(1,t-j+1):t}),\Sigma_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{\max(1,t-j+1):t},\mathbf{u}_{\max(1,t-j+1):t})), so the log-likelihood is available in closed form. For t ≤ j t\leq j , the conditioning window 𝐳 max ⁡ ( 1 , t − j + 1 ) : t \mathbf{z}_{\max(1,t-j+1):t} contains fewer than j j entries; in practice, the decoder left-pads the history with zeros to maintain a fixed input size, consistent with the architecture described in Section H.3 . For trajectory sample 𝐳 1 : T ( s ) \mathbf{z}_{1:T}^{(s)} , we denote the decoder mean and covariance as μ θ ( s ) \displaystyle\mu_{\theta}^{(s)} : = μ θ ( 𝐳 max ⁡ ( 1 , t − j + 1 ) : t ( s ) , 𝐮 max ⁡ ( 1 , t − j + 1 ) : t ) , \displaystyle:=\mu_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{\max(1,t-j+1):t}^{(s)},\mathbf{u}_{\max(1,t-j+1):t}), Σ θ ( s ) \displaystyle\Sigma_{\theta}^{(s)} : = Σ θ ( 𝐳 max ⁡ ( 1 , t − j + 1 ) : t ( s ) , 𝐮 max ⁡ ( 1 , t − j + 1 ) : t ) . \displaystyle:=\Sigma_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{\max(1,t-j+1):t}^{(s)},\mathbf{u}_{\max(1,t-j+1):t}). Using that − log 𝒩 ( 𝐱 t ; μ θ , Σ θ ) = 1 2 [ ( 𝐱 t − μ θ ) ⊤ Σ θ − 1 ( 𝐱 t − μ θ ) + log det ( 2 π Σ θ ) ] , -\log\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_{t};\mu_{\theta},\Sigma_{\theta})=\frac{1}{2}\Big[(\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mu_{\theta})^{\top}\Sigma_{\theta}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mu_{\theta})+\log\det(2\pi\Sigma_{\theta})\Big], if we have diagonal covariance Σ θ \Sigma_{\theta} , this reduces to a weighted squared error plus a log variance term and then − log ⁡ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝐱 t , μ θ , Σ θ ) \displaystyle-\log\mathcal{N}\big(\mathbf{x}_{t};\,\mu_{\theta},\Sigma_{\theta}\big) = 1 2 ​ ∑ i = 1 D [ ( x t , i − μ θ , i ) 2 σ θ , i 2 + log ⁡ ( 2 ​ π ​ σ θ , i 2 ) ] , \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{D}\left[\frac{(x_{t,i}-\mu_{\theta,i})^{2}}{\sigma_{\theta,i}^{2}}+\log(2\pi\sigma_{\theta,i}^{2})\right], Thus we have ℒ recon ( ϕ , θ ; 𝐱 1 : T , 𝐮 1 : T ) \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}}(\phi,\theta;\mathbf{x}_{1:T},\mathbf{u}_{1:T}) = ∑ t = 1 T 𝔼 q ϕ ( 𝐳 1 : T ∣ 𝐱 1 : T , 𝐮 1 : T ) [ − log p θ ( t ) ( 𝐱 t ∣ 𝐳 max ⁡ ( 1 , t − j + 1 ) : t , 𝐮 max ⁡ ( 1 , t − j + 1 ) : t ) ] \displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}_{1:T}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1:T},\mathbf{u}_{1:T})}\Big[-\log p^{(t)}_{\theta}\big(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{z}_{\max(1,t-j+1):t},\mathbf{u}_{\max(1,t-j+1):t}\big)\Big] ≈ 1 S ​ ∑ s = 1 S ∑ t = 1 T [ − log ⁡ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝐱 t , μ θ ( s ) , Σ θ ( s ) ) ] \displaystyle\approx\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Big[-\log\mathcal{N}\big(\mathbf{x}_{t};\,\mu_{\theta}^{(s)},\Sigma_{\theta}^{(s)}\big)\Big] = 1 2 ​ S ​ ∑ s = 1 S ∑ t = 1 T ∑ i = 1 D [ ( x t , i − μ θ , i ( s ) ) 2 σ θ , i ( s ) ​ 2 + log ⁡ ( 2 ​ π ​ σ θ , i ( s ) ​ 2 ) ] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{D}\left[\frac{(x_{t,i}-\mu_{\theta,i}^{(s)})^{2}}{\sigma_{\theta,i}^{(s)2}}+\log(2\pi\sigma_{\theta,i}^{(s)2})\right] : = ℒ recon MC ( ϕ , θ ; 𝐱 1 : T , 𝐮 1 : T ) . \displaystyle:=\mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}}^{\text{MC}}(\phi,\theta;\mathbf{x}_{1:T},\mathbf{u}_{1:T}). sections.heading: Appendix J Extended Related Works
sections.text: Deep state space models. Similarly to other Deep State Space Models (DSSMs) ( Girin et al., 2022 ) , our Diffusion-Driven State Space Model (DDSSM) parametrizes the transitions and emissions densities of a state space model with a neural network. However, our model replaces the parametric (typically Gaussian) transition distribution of a DSSM with a diffusion model. In particular, we extend the Deep Kalman Filter (DKF) of Krishnan et al. (2015) ; Krishnan et al. (2017) to have diffusion transitions. An immediate shortcoming of the usage of Gaussian transitions is the inability to model multi-modal transitions, which we verify in our simulation study in Section 4 . Karl et al. (2016) observed the shortcoming of Gaussian transitions in the context of modeling physical systems, arguing that the regularization provided by Gaussian transitions harms reconstruction performance. Several lines of work have attempted to make the DKF more expressive. Karl et al. (2016) proposed learning a more flexible transition by learning a deterministic transition of a stochastic variable. That is, they learn 𝐳 t = f ψ ​ ( 𝐳 t − 1 , 𝐮 t , β t ) \mathbf{z}_{t}=f_{\psi}(\mathbf{z}_{t-1},\mathbf{u}_{t},\beta_{t}) where f ψ f_{\psi} is a neural network and β t \beta_{t} is a stochastic parameter of the transition sampled from a simple distribution such as a Gaussian. This ensures that the latent states are sampled from the transition distribution, forcing the encoder to receive gradients directly from the transition model. A separate track of work attempting to make the DKF more expressive has been to add auxiliary variables. For example the Kalman VAE (KVAE) ( Fraccaro et al., 2017 ) introduces parameters 𝐚 1 : T \mathbf{a}_{1:T} and propose the generative model p ( 𝐱 1 : T , 𝐚 1 : T , 𝐳 1 : T | 𝐮 1 : T ) = p ( 𝐱 1 : T | 𝐚 1 : T ) p ( 𝐚 1 : T | 𝐳 1 : T ) p ( 𝐳 1 : T | 𝐮 1 : T ) p(\mathbf{x}_{1:T},\mathbf{a}_{1:T},\mathbf{z}_{1:T}|\mathbf{u}_{1:T})=p(\mathbf{x}_{1:T}|\mathbf{a}_{1:T})p(\mathbf{a}_{1:T}|\mathbf{z}_{1:T})p(\mathbf{z}_{1:T}|\mathbf{u}_{1:T}) , relying on linear Gaussian p ⁡ ( 𝐚 t | 𝐳 t , 𝐮 t ) p(\mathbf{a}_{t}|\mathbf{z}_{t},\mathbf{u}_{t}) and p ⁡ ( 𝐳 t | 𝐳 t − 1 , 𝐡 t , 𝐮 t ) p(\mathbf{z}_{t}|\mathbf{z}_{t-1},\mathbf{h}_{t},\mathbf{u}_{t}) distributions. Klushyn et al. (2021) extends this model to have nonlinear Gaussian transitions, proposing the Extended Kalman VAE (EKVAE). The primary advantage to their method is that inference about the parameters 𝐚 t \mathbf{a}_{t} use the filtering/smoothing equations of the extended Kalman filter ( Ribeiro, 2004 ) , to allow the training objective for the transition model to be sample-based instead of likelihood-based. It may be possible to extend the EKVAE and other deep SSMs to use diffusion transitions as well, but we leave this to future work: we emphasize that our contribution is not on the design of the generative model, but rather on the usage of diffusion models as flexible transition distributions. Lastly, we note that several works have extended deep SSMs using normalizing flows (NFs) ( Papamakarios et al., 2021 ) . While these admit exact-likelihoods, they are heavily constrained by the requirement of invertible neural network architectures, limiting applicability across many domains. One recent example is from Chen and Li (2025) , who propose learning a differentiable particle filter ( Le et al., 2017 ) , allowing the transition and emission densities to be parameterized by NFs. We note that diffusion models would be unsuitable for this approach, as the particle filtering algorithm requires many samples through the transition for each time step. Another example is from De Bezenac et al. (2020) , who assume linear transition dynamics and parameterize the emission density with a NF. This enables efficient inference using Kalman-style filtering/smoothing, but does not allow for flexible transition dynamics. We mention Ziegler and Rush (2019) as well, who consider a variety of NF-based approaches for modeling discrete sequences, but they do not consider the true posterior form of their proposed generative models. Models for temporal data which apply diffusion directly in observation space. Several lines of work model temporal data by applying diffusion methods directly in observation space, rather than incorporating a latent dynamic process. The advantage to this approach is that it does not require learning a latent representation of the data, and does not require performing inference about the latent state. For example, Rasul et al. (2021) employs autoregressive forecasting using a diffusion model, by conditioning the diffusion model on a summary of all previous time steps of the series. To create a summary, an RNN is run over the history of the time series, providing a single conditioning variable as an input to their diffusion model. The RNN summary is similar in spirit to the latent state of our model; in our model the conditioning set 𝐜 t \mathbf{c}_{t} fully summarizes the history of the time series up to the time t t . The advantage of our approach is that we are able to operate the diffusion model fully in latent-space, which is by construction well-suited to modeling the dynamics of the time series. Additionally, the latent space can be designed to be low-dimensional, which can make training and sampling more efficient. Another advantage is that our latent representation may provide a more interpretable representation of the dynamics of the time series, whereas it is unclear how to interpret the RNN summary of Rasul et al. (2021) . Another well known work is by Tashiro et al. (2021) , who perform imputation using diffusion models by learning to denoise imputation targets while conditioning on observed data. Their method operates on fixed length windows of a time series, and handles forecasting by setting imputation targets to be future time steps through a conditioning mask. By changing the mask, their method can sample many timesteps into the future by conditioning on a fixed length history. One drawback of this approach is that the model cannot utilize past data beyond the fixed length window which is determined at training time. This is contrary to Rasul et al. (2021) or our method which attempt to infer the necessary parameters to accurately sample the next time step. More importantly, Tashiro et al. (2021) requires their diffusion model to jointly model the full conditional distribution of the entire future given the entire history in a fixed window, which is expensive to learn and sample from. We note that we have designed our diffusion model architecture to match Tashiro et al. (2021) closely, as their previously state-of-the-art performance suggests that their architecture is well-suited to modeling temporal data. We detail the differences between our architecture and theirs in Section H.1 . Latent diffusion models for static data. While diffusion models are already computationally expensive in the static setting—motivating latent diffusion models ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) —the challenge is amplified for time series, where the model must capture both high-dimensional structure and temporal dynamics. Our work can be considered a temporal extension of the diffusion models of Vahdat et al. (2021) and Shmakov et al. (2023) , who train a diffusion model end-to-end in the latent space of a VAE. Like Vahdat et al. (2021) , we design the training objective of the diffusion model to account for the fact the model is being trained concurrently with the VAE. However, we employ preconditioning ( Karras et al., 2022 ) of the denoising model to reduce the variance of the gradients across noise levels. This is important since the gradients of the diffusion model are used to train the VAE. Details of our approach to concurrent training are described in Appendix E . Latent diffusion models for temporal data. (WIP) Qian et al. (2024) propose a latent diffusion model framework for unconditional time-series generation, which they call TimeLDM. They employ a VAE training objective, where the encoder accepts an entire time series as input, and then produces an entire latent time series as output, i.e 𝐳 1 : T = Encoder ( 𝐱 1 : T ) \mathbf{z}_{1:T}=\text{Encoder}(\mathbf{x}_{1:T}) . However, there is no mechanism in their model to capture any temporal structure within 𝒛 1 : T {\bm{z}}_{1:T} . The decoder is responsible for reconstructing the entire time series from the latent time series, and the diffusion model is trained to model the distribution of time-series examples in latent space. We note that their method cannot perform forecasting, and they train in a two-stage manner where the VAE is trained separately from the diffusion model. In comparison, our method does capture temporal structure in the latent space, as the latent state at time t t is conditioned on the latent state at time t − 1 t-1 . Additionally, our model can perform any tasks available to a standard state-space model, including unconditional generation. Suh et al. (2025) proposes a latent diffusion modeling framework to unify forecasting, imputation, unconditional generation, and conditional generation of time series. Their autoencoder similar to Qian et al. (2024) outputs an entire latent time series given an entire time series as input. The decoder however aims to reconstruct a target subset of observations given the latent time series, a conditioning set from the observations, and a mask to indicate which inputs are targets/conditional. The diffusion model is then trained to model the distribution of the latent time series, conditioned on the conditioning set and mask. This is to say that the diffusion model does not operate independently of the data, contrary to our method where the diffusion model lives fully in the latent space, conditioning only on latent features. The strongest similarity which Suh et al. (2025) has to our method is that their method constructs a full ELBO training objective to maximize the log-likelihood of the data, where the loss of the diffusion model is a component of the ELBO. Of interest is the observation that end-to-end training was detrimental to their model, instead they prefer first training the autoencoder and then training the diffusion model separately. This claim however is not validated within their paper, and it is unclear how they attempted to train end-to-end. As an artifact of training in stages, their variational posterior is regularized towards a standard Gaussian distribution. If training jointly, their objective instead would regularize the variational posterior towards the distribution of the diffusion model. Liu et al. (2024) and Feng et al. (2024) give other approaches to time-series diffusion modeling in the latent space of a pre-trained autoencoder. We note that Feng et al. (2024) applies regularization of the latent space during the training of the autoencoder to a standard Gaussian distribution to avoid learning an unregularized space.

Existing approaches typically sacrifice one of these goals: deep state space models often assume Gaussian latent transitions, limiting fit and forecasting, while diffusion models are highly expressive but lack principled inference for the underlying dynamics. To combine the strengths of both, we introduce the Diffusion-Driven State Space Model (DDSSM), which replaces the conventional Gaussian transition distribution with a diffusion model. Our DDSSM resolves the open problem of how to jointly train an autoencoder and a diffusion model on sequential data, thereby extending the literature on latent diffusion models for time series. Moreover, we find that the DDSSM empirically outperforms a state-of-the-art deep SSM at fitting and forecasting a simulated time series with multimodal transitions. 1 Introduction Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ) have emerged as a powerful class of generative models for high-dimensional data. For time series data, emerging evidence demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on forecasting, imputation, and sample-generation tasks ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , where diffusion models are typically used as generative samplers to produce future trajectories conditioned on past observations ( Su et al., 2025 ) . Some approaches perform diffusion directly in observation space ( Tashiro et al., 2021 ; Rasul et al., 2021 ; Kollovieh et al., 2023 ; Price et al., 2025 ) , while others apply diffusion in the latent space of an autoencoder ( Feng et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Blattmann et al., 2023 ) , which can improve tractability for high-dimensional data. However, existing latent time-series diffusion methods typically rely on two-stage training: first learning the autoencoder, then training the diffusion model. This may produce an over-regularized latent space ( Liu et al., 2024 ) that discards information needed for downstream generative dynamics, consistent with research on latent diffusion for static data where two-stage training leads to poorer representations and generative performance ( Vahdat et al., 2021 ; Shmakov et al., 2023 ) . In contrast, State Space Models (SSMs) ( Kalman, 1960 ; Shumway and Stoffer, 1982 ; Durbin and Koopman, 2001 ) provide a classical framework for temporal data that naturally supports end-to-end training, captures timestep-by-timestep dynamics, and admits well-studied extensions to diverse settings. SSMs typically assume observed data are generated from latent states that evolve over time via a Markov process, with each observation depending on the current state. Classically, the linear Gaussian state-space model assumes first-order Markovian linear dynamics and linear Gaussian observation models ( Roweis and Ghahramani, 1999 ) . To absolve linearity, transition and emission densities may be parameterized with deep neural networks ( Krishnan et al., 2015 ; Krishnan et al., 2017 ) , where training is performed via stochastic backpropagation ( Rezende et al., 2014 ; Kingma and Welling, 2014 ) . These neural-network-parameterized SSMs may be referred to as Deep SSMs, or Dynamical Variational Autoencoders (DVAEs); see Girin et al. (2022) for a review. While neural-networks allow the mean of each latent state to be a nonlinear function of the previous latent state, the transition densities in these models assume some parametric form ( Karl et al., 2016 ) , most often Gaussian ( Krishnan et al., 2015 ; Johnson et al., 2016 ; Fraccaro et al., 2017 ; Krishnan et al., 2017 ; Ansari et al., 2021 ; Girin et al., 2022 ; Revach et al., 2022 ; Dowling et al., 2024 ; Hashempoorikderi and Choi, 2024 ; Chinellato and Marcuzzi, 2025 ) , thereby limiting their expressivity. Moreover, Gaussian transition densities induce a Gaussian prior on the latent trajectories. Within the VAE framework the Gaussian prior is known to over-regularize, yielding latent representations that poorly represent the structure of the data ( Tomczak and Welling, 2018 ; Klushyn et al., 2019 ; Chen et al., 2017 ) . Inspired by the framework of composing probabilistic graphical models with neural networks ( Johnson et al., 2016 ) , we propose to get the “best of both worlds” by composing SSMs with diffusion models. Our diffusion-driven SSMs (DDSSMs) naturally model the real-time dynamics of a system without imposing restrictive Gaussian assumptions about its latent dynamics. Further, we adapt SSM ideas to resolve the open problem of how to jointly train an autoencoder and a diffusion model on sequential data in a principled manner. In this way, we extend latent diffusion models for time series. 2 Method Generative Model. Similarly to other Deep State Space Models (DSSMs) ( Girin et al., 2022 ) such as the Deep Kalman Filter (DKF) ( Krishnan et al., 2015 ; Krishnan et al., 2017 ) , our Diffusion-Driven State Space Model (DDSSM) parametrizes the transitions and emissions densities of a state space model with a neural network. However, our model replaces the parametric (typically Gaussian) transition distribution of a DSSM with a diffusion model. This design enables complex, potentially multi-modal transition dynamics (validated in Section 4 ) and avoids the restrictive regularization of Gaussian transitions ( Karl et al., 2016 ) . Integration with advances such as the extended Kalman filter VAE ( Klushyn et al., 2021 ) is left for future work. Diffusion models for temporal data. Some works ( Rasul et al., 2021 ; Tashiro et al., 2021 ; Kollovieh et al., 2023 ) apply diffusion directly in observation space, but the high computational cost of diffusion – motivating latent diffusion for static data ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) – is exacerbated in time series due to the need to model both high-dimensional structure and temporal dynamics. This has led to latent diffusion approaches for time series ( Qian et al., 2024 ; Suh et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Feng et al., 2024 ) , which typically rely on two-stage training (autoencoder then diffusion), potentially yielding over-regularized latent spaces that discard information needed for generative dynamics ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Vahdat et al., 2021 ; Shmakov et al., 2023 ) . Our approach instead follows Vahdat et al. (2021) and Shmakov et al. (2023) by training diffusion end-to-end in latent space, extended here to the temporal setting.
